summary: Describes how the core XMPP protocol is used to provide basic instant messaging and presence, the functionality laid out in RFC 2779. It covers things like contact lists and showing whether someone is available. It was replaced by RFC 6121.

eli5.summary: Chat apps show who is online and let you send them a message. This memo says how XMPP does both, such as keeping your friends list and showing a green light.

subtitle: How chat apps handle friend lists, status, and who sees your availability.

tldr.problem: XMPP provides the raw stream and transport, but applications need standardized ways to send messages, show online status, and manage contact relationships.
tldr.mechanism: This memo defines how to use XMPP stanzas for instant messaging, presence broadcasting, subscription-based privacy, roster management (contact lists), and blocking unwanted communications.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3921 was later consolidated and replaced by RFC 6121, which combined core XMPP functionality with instant messaging and presence into a single specification.

facts.label: Presence show values
facts.value: away, chat (actively interested), dnd (do not disturb), xa (extended away)

facts.label: Subscription states
facts.value: none, to (you see them), from (they see you), both (mutual)

facts.label: Priority range
facts.value: -128 to +127 for routing messages to the highest-priority client

today: RFC 3921 defined how to do IM and presence in XMPP. It was consolidated into RFC 6121, which merged the core protocol and IM/presence into one specification, making XMPP easier to implement uniformly.

sections.title: Building Chat on XMPP
sections.content: The core XMPP specification (RFC 3920) defines XML streams, TLS security, SASL authentication, and three stanza types: message, presence, and IQ. This memo describes how to extend and apply those primitives to build instant messaging (IM) and presence applications—basically, how to turn XMPP into a working chat system that meets the requirements of RFC 2779. The core provides the transport; this memo provides the chat-specific rules.
sections.eli5: XMPP is like mail. This memo is how to use it for group chat and showing when friends are online.

sections.title: Messages and Presence Stanzas
sections.content: Messages come in five types: chat (one-to-one conversation), normal (standalone message), groupchat (multi-user chat room), headline (automated alert), and error (error report). A message stanza MAY contain a subject, body, and thread ID. Presence stanzas broadcast availability and can have types like subscribe (request to see someone's status), subscribed (approve that request), and unavailable (going offline). Presence can include a show field (away, chat, dnd, xa), a status message, and a priority number for routing when a user has multiple clients.
sections.eli5: Messages say what you want to say. Presence says whether you are here and what you are doing (busy, away, online).

sections.title: Contact Lists and Subscriptions
sections.content: In XMPP, your contact list is called a roster. Each contact is identified by a JID (Jabber ID, like user@example.com). The server stores the roster on your behalf so you can access it from any client. When you add a contact, you request a subscription to their presence; they can approve or deny it. The subscription state tells you whether you can see their presence, they can see yours, or both (called 'to', 'from', or 'both'). Each roster item can have a nickname and belong to groups. You can add, update, and delete roster items at any time; the server pushes changes to all your available clients.
sections.eli5: Your roster is your friends list. When you add someone, you ask to see their status. They say yes or no. Then you can see them online or offline.

sections.title: How Presence Works
sections.content: Presence follows a broadcast model. When you come online, you send initial presence (no type, no 'to' attribute). Your server sends presence probes to all contacts you subscribe to, then broadcasts your presence to all contacts subscribed to you. When you go offline, you send unavailable presence, and your server broadcasts that too. You can also send directed presence to a single contact (useful for showing status to someone outside your roster). Presence subscriptions are durable: they persist across sessions until explicitly canceled. The RFC specifies exact server rules for when to send presence and to whom, including blocking-aware rules for privacy.
sections.eli5: When you log in, the app tells everyone on your friends list. When you log out, it tells them you left. If someone new adds you, you have to say yes or no before they see you.

sections.title: Privacy: Subscriptions and Blocking
sections.content: Privacy is built into the subscription model. No one sees your presence unless you approve their subscription request. The RFC also defines blocking: a user can block specific JIDs to prevent them from receiving outbound presence notifications or inbound messages. Blocking is separate from roster management (you can block someone on your roster) and persists across sessions. The server enforces blocking rules when routing presence and message stanzas. A blocked contact cannot see your status changes and cannot deliver messages to you, though the RFC leaves some implementation details to servers.
sections.eli5: You control who sees you online by approving or denying subscription requests. You can also block people entirely so they cannot reach you.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: The RFC specifies that all communication should use TLS and SASL (both defined in XMPP Core). Servers must validate that roster pushes come from the server or the user's own JID, not from spoofed sources. Subscription and presence stanzas can be spoofed if not authenticated, so clients should validate server-sourced data. The blocking mechanism is advisory: a blocked contact can still attempt to message you, but the server must not deliver those messages. The RFC does not mandate offline message storage, so undelivered messages may be lost.
sections.eli5: Encrypt your connection. Do not trust friend requests if they do not come from the real server. A blocked person can still try to message you, but the server will ignore them.
